definition: [Charpente] Any combination and assembly of large-section timber for building. NOTE: Viollet's opening definition: 'toute combinaison et assemblage de bois de gros echantillon'.
[Charpente] The triangulated transverse frame of a roof. Viollet says the Greeks already knew it. NOTE: ferme-maîtresse = principal truss; ferme de croupe = hip truss.
[Charpente] A fully armed truss with tie and king-post, as opposed to the chevrons between. NOTE: At Notre-Dame the hip fermes-maîtresses are 'accouplees' (doubled/paired).

[Charpente] The repeated rafter between trusses. NOTE: French Gothic chevrons are individually framed - see chevron portant ferme. || [Maison] In the Vosges the middle pan de bois supports the upper ends of the rafters; in the Nivernais the projecting joists frame into the rafters.

english: rafter-couple framed as its own truss ('rafter carrying truss')
definition: [Charpente] A rafter pair armed almost like a ferme - collar, jambettes, contre-fiches - but with NO tie at its base and usually no king-post; it stands on patins/blochets assembled in the double wall-plates. NOTE: Names the whole 13th-c French system: 'charpentes à chevrons portant fermes'. This is the key French/English divergence.
[Charpente] The main inclined member of a ferme. NOTE: In the French Gothic system its OUTER face lies in the same plane as the chevrons.

[Charpente] A second inclined member set below and parallel to the arbalétrier, keeping the king-post in plane and stiffening the truss. NOTE: At Reims the sous-arbalétriers are moises (paired), one piece each, 14.50 m long, and are 'toute sa force'.

[Charpente] The bottom chord. Viollet's doctrine: its ONLY function is to stop the rafters spreading; it must carry NOTHING and must itself be suspended from the king-post at mid-span. NOTE: The whole polemic against English practice hangs on this. || [Maison] Received by the main beam where it passes through the Chateaudun front wall.

VERIFICATION CORRECTED. A tie set higher up the truss to stop the rafters bending. The reader's note 'Viollet places them at EQUAL intervals up the rafter - a buckling-length rule' is NOT a rule: 'a intervalles egaux' occurs once in the whole article and is scoped to one truss - 'La flexion des arbaletriers DE CETTE FERME est donc arretee a intervalles egaux par les trois entraits retrousses' (the Notre-Dame hip truss, fig. 9). At Reims the ferme's two collars sit 3.39 m and 6.09 m from the head of a 17.08 m rafter, leaving the lower 10.99 m with none: intervals 3.39 / 2.70 / 10.99 m. || SOURCE ENTRIES: [Charpente] A tie set higher up the truss, stopping the rafters bending. NOTE: Viollet places them at EQUAL intervals up the rafter - a buckling-length rule.

[Charpente] Two pieces crossed as a St-Andrew cross, halved together, used instead of a tie when a barrel vault crown blocks the tie line. NOTE: Viollet records these as a failure: the tenons tear out.

english: king post; also the carved ridge terminal
definition: The central vertical hanging post; gathers the rafter heads and SUSPENDS the tie at mid-span. A faux poincon does not reach a tie. In the Norman/Norse tradition the word also means the carved terminal at each end of a ridge, the two joined over the roof by a crested board (Bayeux tapestry; surviving in the Eure). VERIFICATION NOTE on Auxerre: the text says only 'un octogone de 0,13 centimetres de diametre' (meaning 0 m 13 c = 0.13 m) - it does NOT distinguish across-flats from across-corners, so drop the reader's 'across flats'. || SOURCE ENTRIES: [Charpente] The central vertical hanging post; suspends the tie and gathers the rafter heads. NOTE: At Auxerre its visible length is an OCTAGON 0.13 m across with a small carved capital. || [Maison] In the Norman/Norse tradition the two ends of the ridge carry richly decorated poincons joined over the roof by a timber cut as a crest.
[Charpente] A king-post that does not reach down to a tie. NOTE: Standard in the Anglo-Norman tie-less trusses (Ely, Westminster).
[Charpente] Viollet's French rendering of the ENGLISH term, used when describing 13th-c English trusses where the tie carries the post. NOTE: He cites the name only to condemn the practice.

[Charpente] The longitudinal plate on the wall head. Normally DOUBLE and laid flat rather than square. NOTE: The double sablière is the French positioning member: the tie is dovetailed into both, and the blochet is notched over both. || [Maison] At Annonay the first-floor front is 'compose sur la face anterieure de trois sablieres superposees, jointives, sur lesquelles s'assemblent les montants'. NOTE: At Laval the jetty rests on three corbelled sablieres; at Nantua the sablieres under the roof are doubled.
[Charpente] A plate laid under the sablière receiving the tie ends and pegged to it. NOTE: Saint-Ouen de Rouen, exceptional.

[Charpente] A short horizontal timber lying across the wall plates into which the rafter foot and the jambette are tenoned. NOTE: In the Anglo-Norman system it grows into a projecting cantilever carrying posts - i.e. the hammer-beam. Viollet uses the same word for both.
[Charpente] Viollet: 'D est le patin ou blochet'. NOTE: Treat as an exact synonym.

english: ashlar-piece / short strut from blochet to rafter
definition: [Charpente] Short post, vertical or slightly raked, tenoned into the blochet and the tie and housed into the rafter. NOTE: RULE: 'plus les combles sont aigus, plus les jambettes se rapprochent de la verticale'; raked ones resist the rafter thrust better.
[Charpente] The same piece cut on a curve so that it forms part of the visible boarded barrel. NOTE: Auxerre, Mauvesin, Châlons, Sully.

english: brace / tie-brace / brace, strut (timber) / curved brace
definition: [Charpente] An inclined brace; in the corrected truss it is footed in the KING POST and heads on the rafter, so it does not load the tie. NOTE: Contrast with jambette, which loads the tie. || [Escalier] 'Le limon est soulage dans sa partie par un gousset I et un lien K. Les grands liens sont surtout necessaires pour empecher le roulement et les poussees.' NOTE: 6 occurrences; also the short braces under the pivoting stair's treads. || [Maison] Eases the projecting ends of sablieres and purlins; at Reims the jambe-etriere receives two liens, carved with Samson and Saint Michael.

english: angle brace, strut between a horizontal and an inclined member
definition: [Charpente] Short brace triangulating a corner. NOTE: Viollet spells it 'esselier' throughout this article.

[Charpente] Compression strut running from a lower member up to the arbalétrier, often set PERPENDICULAR to it, and often carrying a purlin course. NOTE: Stopped from sliding by a renfort left in the solid of the rafter plus moises.
[Charpente] The heavy raking strut at the base of the truss, footing the lower contre-fiche. NOTE: With the hanging moises it makes the base self-tightening under load.

english: clamping pair of side-pieces tightened by wooden keys
definition: Two timbers laid one each side of other members and tightened by wooden keys (clefs de bois) so several members act as one. THE characteristic French device. VERIFICATION NOTE: a moise is BY DEFINITION a pair, and Viollet counts cheeks individually ('Le second entrait retrousse I se compose de deux moises qui embrassent ces memes pieces'; 'deux paires de moises verticales N'). So the Reims sous-arbaletriers-moises are 2 PAIRS = 4 cheeks, and 'd'un seul morceau' in 'ces sous-arbaletriers-moises I qui sont d'un seul morceau et n'ont pas moins de 14 m ,50 de longueur' means each timber is UNSPLICED over its whole length - a timber-sourcing feat, compare his Westminster admission 'nous n'avons pu savoir s'ils sont d'un seul morceau' - not that the moise is one piece. Variants: moises pendantes (hanging, waisted between the keys because they work only in tension), sous-arbaletriers-moises, courbes moises, petites moises. || SOURCE ENTRIES: [Charpente] Two timbers laid one on each side of other members and tightened by wooden keys, so several members act as one. NOTE: The single most characteristic French device. Variants: moises pendantes (hanging), sous-arbalétriers-moises, courbes moises (curved clamps at Westminster), petites moises.
[Charpente] A pair of moises hung from the rafter or king-post to suspend the tie at intermediate points. NOTE: Lightened (élégi) between the keys because they act only in tension.
[Charpente] The key driven through a moise to tighten it. NOTE: Reims uses several keys per moise; the whole roof has no ironwork.
[Charpente] Square-headed iron pin. NOTE: Saint-Ouen de Rouen - an early appearance of iron in a French roof.
[Charpente] The peg through a tenon. NOTE: Rafters are held to ridge, purlins and plates 'par des chevilles de chêne'.

[Charpente] Longitudinal member carrying the rafters. NOTE: THE regional test: in France it is either laid ON the rafter (early, wasteful of wall), or set UNDER it / into it (later); in the Anglo-Norman system it is locked between rafter and curved brace, forming a grillage with them.
[Charpente] The cleat nailed/pegged on the principal rafter that stops a purlin laid on top from sliding. NOTE: Only needed in the antique system where pannes sit on top.

[Charpente] A true ridge into which the rafter heads are tenoned. NOTE: Rare - Mauvesin has one; most 13th-14th c French roofs have none. || [Maison] Lead ridges at Bourges, formerly gilt and painted.

english: under-ridge / collar-purlin at the king-post heads
definition: [Charpente] A longitudinal piece at the head of the king-posts on which the rafter heads, halved together, rest. NOTE: Distinct from faîtage. Viollet notes the Notre-Dame choir roof has NEITHER faîtage NOR pannes.
[Charpente] Horizontal piece running truss to truss, usually paired with St-Andrew crosses. NOTE: Also used for the axial pieces under an enrayure.

english: St Andrew's cross / X-brace / St Andrew's cross bracing
definition: [Charpente] Crossed diagonal bracing, halved together, in the LONGITUDINAL plane, keeping the trusses plumb and the sous-faîte level. NOTE: Also used in the plane of the rafters (Hargnies) and in the aprons of a pan-de-bois. || [Maison] In the alleges they 'empechaient le deversement des poteaux d'huisseries' - stop the jamb-posts leaning out. NOTE: Reims 26bis is a deliberate counter-example: no crosses at all in the whole height.

[Charpente] A long diagonal brace. At Sully the écharpes croisees are lapped à tiers-bois on the OUTSIDE of the rafters, in the plane of the roof slope. NOTE: Viollet says it is chiefly these that stop the roof 'rolling'.
[Charpente] Pieces laid on the rafters to make up the step formed by the crossed écharpes before the boarding is laid. NOTE: Sully-sur-Loire.

english: gusset / knee brace / gusset, bracket (timber); also the small corner squinch
definition: [Charpente] Brace assembled into the contre-fiche and into the purlin, stopping the purlin sagging between trusses. NOTE: Amiens, and the fig.15/15bis family. Also stops the hiement. || [Escalier] 11 occurrences. In timber: 'le gousset du limon de depart', 'un gousset embreve dans les montants'. In stone: 'ces trompes, ou ces goussets plutot, sont appareilles d'une seule pierre'. NOTE: Same word for the stone corner filler and the timber angle bracket.

english: racking of trusses and rafters under wind
definition: [Charpente] Viollet's own footnote: 'On appelle hiement, en termes de charpenterie, le mouvement que l'effort du vent imprime aux fermes et chevrons.' NOTE: This is a direct, quotable definition of the wind-load failure mode - gold for a structural rule.

english: rolling (longitudinal racking of the whole roof)
definition: [Charpente] The whole frame leaning/travelling along its length. NOTE: Resisted by liens into the axial entretoises, by St-Andrew crosses, and above all by roof-plane écharpes.
[Charpente] A truss falling out of its vertical plane. NOTE: Resisted by liens, sous-arbalétriers, crosses, and by the boarding.

english: horizontal radiating frame of a hip or conical roof / horizontal framing ring / grillage of beams
definition: [Charpente] The ring of ties, angle-ties and trimmers at one level of a hip/cone; a conical roof has three or more, stacked. NOTE: The prolonged blochets of the rafters form the lowest one. || [Maison] At Annonay a thick fir enrayure sits on the masonry ground floor, its third course forming the floor and oversailing to carry the jetty.
[Charpente] Diagonal member of an enrayure taking goussets like a tie. NOTE: Conical roofs, second enrayure.

[Charpente] Piece tenoned between rafters to receive the heads of the faux chevrons. NOTE: Printed with a cedilla, 'linçoirs'; in the text 'les linçoirs I, détaillés en I′, I″ et I‴'. Its stated purpose is to make ERECTION possible.
[Charpente] A lighter rafter between the true chevrons in the lower zone of a cone, only to support the boarding. NOTE: Stops at the second enrayure, because the cone narrows.

[Charpente] Short piece extending the roof plane past the wall to throw water clear. NOTE: At Sully great coyaux roof the machicolated wall-walks; at Mauvesin the chevrons themselves do the coyau's job.

english: tilting fillet / batten under the boarding
definition: [Charpente] Batten laid between rafters under the volige to stiffen it. NOTE: Hargnies.

english: thin boarding under the tiles or slates
definition: [Charpente] Sheathing boards. NOTE: At Notre-Dame the oak volige is what actually keeps the rafters in plane - remove it and you can move the trusses by hand. At Messine it is DOUBLE and laid crossways.
[Charpente] The thin riven oak boards nailed on the courbes to form the visible barrel ceiling; 0.01 m, sometimes 0.009 m thick. NOTE: Jointed 'a grain d'orge' to keep wind out; generally painted.

english: cover strip / batten over a board joint
definition: [Charpente] Moulded strip hiding the bardeau joints, stiffening the courbes and serving as decoration. NOTE: Two sizes, gros and petits, at Hargnies.
[Charpente] The edge profile used between bardeaux so that wind driven under the tiles cannot enter. NOTE: fig.22.

english: boarded lining / wainscot ceiling / boarding, panelling / boarded
definition: [Charpente] The visible boarded barrel under an apparent roof. NOTE: Sully, Auxerre, Palais de la Cite. || [Maison] The Provins hotel hall is 'recouverte par une charpente apparente lambrissee en berceau' - an exposed roof boarded as a barrel.

VERIFICATION CORRECTED on the span figure. A member cut or grown to a curve. The reader's note made 5.40 m 'the threshold above which two stacked courbes are needed'; the text states only that THIS truss has 5.40 m of span ('Cette ferme n'a que 5 m ,40 de portee') and that for greater spans one-piece courbes were hard to find ('lorsque les portees etaient plus grandes, il eut ete difficile de trouver des courbes d'un seul morceau'). No threshold is stated - treat 5.40 m as the span of the fig. 28 example. || SOURCE ENTRIES: [Charpente] A member cut or grown to a curve; in the ceiling barrels a run of them makes the arc, in the Anglo-Norman trusses one huge courbe replaces the tie's function. NOTE: Availability limits span: above about 5.40 m you cannot get a single courbe and must stack two.
[Charpente] Planks rebated into rafter and curve to fill the spandrel and make the two act together. NOTE: Ely.

english: open tracery infill / openwork, open screen / open-work, tracery screen
definition: [Charpente] Traceried panels filling every void between the main members. NOTE: Westminster - Viollet insists they are STRUCTURAL (vertical 'ordonnees' preventing the curves deforming). || [Escalier] 'des vis enfermees dans des cages en partie ou totalement a claire-voie'. NOTE: The type at Notre-Dame de Paris, Mainz, Laon, Reims.
[Charpente] A key sunk in the thickness of the timbers holding pieces together invisibly. NOTE: Malvern; paired with 'languettes' (tongues).
[Charpente] The joint by which the tie ends grip the double wall-plates. NOTE: Resists the outward push of the rafters on the plates.

english: housed shouldered abutment / a shallow housing/rebate at a joint
definition: [Charpente] A housing cut so an inclined member's shoulder bears solidly, not just its tenon. NOTE: Jambettes are ALWAYS embrévés into the rafters. || [Escalier] 'sera legerement embrevee dans le limon en E'; 'un gousset embreve dans les montants'. NOTE: The joint that stops a tenoned member rotating.

english: boss / shoulder left standing in the solid / thickening, enlarged block on a post or limon / nib, reinforcement left in a springer
definition: [Charpente] Extra timber deliberately left on a rafter to give a housing more bearing 'sans affamer le bois'. NOTE: Also used to stop a purlin sliding. || [Escalier] Mortised to receive the balustrade posts, or to receive the poutrelle de buttee. NOTE: fig.26 H, fig.28 N. || [Construction -- Voutes] A projection left in a springer course behind the freed voussoirs to receive the web. NOTE: Named on fig. 49 bis.
[Charpente] To cut a housing so deep that the member loses its strength. NOTE: The stated reason for the renfort.
[Charpente] Two members each cut half away and lapped. NOTE: Rafter heads at the ridge, St-Andrew crosses, false ties.
[Charpente] Lapped at one third the depth. NOTE: The crossed écharpes at Sully, laid outside the rafters.
[Charpente] Section cut away where the member only works in tension, keeping full section at the joints. NOTE: Hanging moises; the false ties over the Burgundian barrels.
[Charpente] The squared cross-section of a timber. NOTE: Viollet's whole historical thesis is about équarrissage shrinking as combination improves.

english: timber squared from a single whole tree
definition: [Charpente] As opposed to bois de sciage (sawn from a larger log); hewn with the axe and cleared of sapwood. NOTE: Sully: 'tous ces bois sont des bois de brin et non de sciage, equarris a la hache' - the stated reason for 500 years' survival.

english: sapwood / sapwood / wane / shake or check / to warp
definition: [Charpente] Removed from the timber. NOTE: Durability rule. || [Escalier] The defects the conversion method avoids: sapwood and wane end up in the tail of the step; the saw cuts follow the direction of the shakes so the step cannot check or warp. NOTE: A materials rule, useful for texturing as well as for lore.
[Charpente] Timber squared to sharp edges with no waney edge. NOTE: Chartres, Reims - a quality marker.

english: dwarf wall / wall head above the vaults
definition: [Charpente] The low masonry wall on the extrados of the wall ribs and window arches on which the roof plates sit; its thickness cannot exceed the diameter of the piers below. NOTE: Reduced to about 1 m - the constraint that forced the whole 13th-c French system.

[Charpente] The side wall carrying the gutter and the roof plates. NOTE: Raised in Burgundy so a tie could pass over the barrel crowns. || [Maison] The wall under the eaves, as opposed to the gable wall. Alleys between houses forced the goutterots onto the alleys and the pignons onto the street.

[Charpente] The channel on the wall head. NOTE: Where absent, the eaves rely on coyaux (Mauvesin). || [Maison] Of stone in Burgundy and haute Champagne from the mid-13th c, sloped to two end gargoyles on projecting corbels; elsewhere hollowed in a beam or made of lead-covered boards.
[Charpente] The hipped end of a roof; here over the chevet. NOTE: Circular croupe = the basis of the conical tower roof.
[Charpente] The internal angle between two roof slopes. NOTE: Mentioned for the spire base: 'suspendre au-dessus des fermes des noues'.
[Charpente] The rafter head cut to a long splay where rafters converge on the apex of a cone. NOTE: fig.36 quater.
[Charpente] The erection operation; tenons must be enterable in the chosen order. NOTE: Explicit design constraint for conical roofs.

english: the carpenter's art of geometrical setting-out
definition: [Charpente] The layout/stereotomy tradition of the carpenters' corporation. NOTE: Viollet: the guild was 'instruite dans l'art du trait' and kept its traditions long after the Renaissance.
[Charpente] A floor beam stiffened by a curved or straight auxiliary piece, tied to it with iron bolts and cotters. NOTE: Amiens organ loft ~15 m span; Blain; hotel de la Tremoille ~12 m.
[Charpente] The key locking an iron bolt. NOTE: The only structural iron Viollet accepts as medieval French practice.
[Charpente] The wider member of an armed beam, forming the seat for the joists. NOTE: Blain.
[Charpente] Floor joist, usually left exposed. NOTE: Medieval floors: 'peu ou point d'enchevêtrures'.
[Charpente] Framing round an opening. NOTE: Viollet says medieval floors have few or none - a strong simplicity rule for floor generators.
[Charpente] The framed wall of a timber house. NOTE: Bay module = one principal post per floor beam.

[Charpente] Vertical member; poteau principal over a beam, poteau (secondary) between. NOTE: Also the posts standing on the hammer-beams at Westminster. || [Escalier] The corner posts of a timber stair, 0,18 x 0,20 m, set on edge in the direction of the emmarchement, running from foundation to head on a stone parpaing. NOTE: Distinguish from montant (the post carrying one step in a joinery vis).
[Charpente] A short post relieving a plate or a brace. NOTE: Chartres house; Ely (carved as a shaft).
[Charpente] The plate over the secondary posts, tenoned into the principal posts. NOTE: Chartres house.

english: apron panel below a window / window apron / breast below the sill
definition: [Charpente] The panel between sill and floor, braced with St-Andrew crosses and filled with light masonry. NOTE: Chartres house. || [Maison] Where the St Andrew crosses go, and where the masonry hourdis later hides behind joinery panels. NOTE: In Burgundy a cellar entrance can be cut under the allege of a ground-floor window.
[Charpente] The heavy beam over a shopfront carrying the first-floor joists. NOTE: fig.38.

english: the medieval name for jettied oversailing storeys
definition: [Charpente] Successive corbelled projections of each storey over the street, gaining one to three feet a floor. NOTE: 'ces encorbellements, que l'on appelait ligneaux' - a rare period term.
[Charpente] Little corbel built into the wall to take a brace foot. NOTE: Ely.

[Charpente] The lower framed stage of a timber spire, carried above the valley trusses so as not to load the transverse arches. NOTE: Notre-Dame's, raised by about 1230, is Viollet's model of 13th-c skill.
[Charpente] Used in northern France until about the beginning of the 12th c, and only workable on a FLAT roof. NOTE: So: tile type dates and constrains pitch.
[Charpente] Used where a Romanesque gable is too steep for Roman tile. NOTE: The exception that lets a steep Romanesque roof exist.
[Charpente] The present covering at Messina. NOTE: Viollet thinks the original was Roman tile.

[Escalier] The generic modern term Viollet uses throughout. NOTE: Sauval states the word was NOT current in the Middle Ages: 'puisqu'en ce temps-la le nom d'escalier n'etait pas connu'. The medieval word for a spiral stair is vis; a flight is a degre or a rampe.

[Escalier] Given as the headword synonym: 'ESCALIER, s. m. Degre.' In palaces the great external stair was called le degre par excellence. NOTE: Also used for an individual step and for a whole stair; context decides.

[Escalier] The helical stair turning about a central axis. The standard medieval term. Joinville: 'il tenoient leur parlement en une viz qui descendoit de l'une chambre en l'autre'. NOTE: 'la grande vis du Louvre' is how Sauval names the state stair. Use vis, not escalier, for medieval naming.

french: escalier a vis / escalier en limacon
english: spiral stair / winding stair (lit. snail) / spiral stair (newel stair)
definition: [Escalier] Viollet's two names for the same thing: 'on eut donc recours a l'escalier a vis ou en limacon'. NOTE: limacon appears once, at the introduction of the type. || [Maison] In Burgundy it is planted in the street wall itself and serves as the ground-floor vestibule. NOTE: 'ajoure' at Chateaudun means open-work / pierced.
[Escalier] A stair made of straight flights, as opposed to one with winders. NOTE: One of the three axes of the opening taxonomy.
[Escalier] A stair whose steps are girons, i.e. wedge-shaped winders. NOTE: Paired with 'a vis' in the taxonomy.

english: flight (of a stair); also the raking run
definition: [Escalier] The sloping run between landings. 'La rampe avait nom epuiement.' NOTE: 39 occurrences — the article's main word for a flight. Do not translate as handrail here.

[Escalier] The medieval name for the rampe of a great external stair, evidenced by a XIII c. verse quoted by Viollet: 'El pales vint, l'epuiement / De sanc le truva tut sanglant.' NOTE: From the Lai d'Ywenec, poesies de Marie de France. Rare and valuable naming datum.
[Escalier] The individual step. 141 occurrences. NOTE: In stone vis work a marche is normally ONE stone comprising tread + newel segment + wall bearing.

english: to wind, to form winders / to wind (of a stair), to set out the treads
definition: [Escalier] Verb: the steps giron in a cylinder. 'comme si elles gironnaient dans un cylindre'; 'les deux rampes gironnant l'une au-dessus de l'autre'. NOTE: Precise generator verb: to lay treads radially about an axis. || [Maison] 'a gauche ou a droite, selon que gironne l'escalier, est la porte C' - the hand of the stair decides which side the door goes. NOTE: A real generator constraint: door side is a function of stair handedness.

english: length of a step / clear width of a stair - but see the fig. 6 exception
definition: VERIFICATION CORRECTED. Normally the step's usable length, i.e. the stair's clear width: 'Ces sortes d'escaliers ne depassent guere 1 m ,00 c. d'emmarchement'; 'il en est dont les emmarchements n'ont que 0,50 c.; les plus grands n'ont pas plus de 2 m ,00'; 'les poteaux ... poses de champ dans le sens de l'emmarchement'. The 1.00 m figure is confirmed arithmetically by Viollet himself (1.90 m cage less at least 0.325 m of newel leaves 0.80 m max per step). BUT in the fig. 6 wedge-step passage it means the GOING at one end: 'deux marches eussent ensemble 0,30 c. de hauteur et chacune 0,30 c. d'emmarchement par un bout, ce qui permettait d'inscrire la rampe dans un angle de 45 degres' - and the plate proves it, because the 0,30 arrow lies along a-b and the companion drawing is lettered 'Elevat. sur a.b'. Do NOT feed a generator a single meaning. Also strike the reader's claim that all five occurrences carry a dimension: two do not. || SOURCE ENTRIES: [Escalier] The width of the going, i.e. the length of a step available to walk on. 'Ces sortes d'escaliers ne depassent guere 1m,00 c. d'emmarchement.' NOTE: 5 occurrences and every one carries a dimension — the single most useful parameter word in the article.

english: newel, the central shaft of a spiral stair
definition: [Escalier] The core about which the winders turn. 51 occurrences. Can be (a) a stack of separate drums carrying a helical vault, (b) an assembly of segments each integral with a step, (c) coursed masonry with the steps housed in, (d) big stones set en delit, or (e) in timber, one shaft with mortises up the rake. NOTE: Sauval calls it a colonne ('vis tournante a double colonne (noyau)'); Viollet glosses this.

[Escalier] Used for a timber or monolithic newel: 'un arbre ou noyau a pivot'; 'les morceaux superposes de cet arbre de pierre'. NOTE: 3 occurrences; the pivoting stair's rotating shaft is the arbre O.

[Escalier] The enclosure the stair stands in: 'les cages cylindriques n'ayant que six pieds'; 'posee dans des cages comprises dans les constructions ou accolees a ces constructions'. NOTE: 15 occurrences. Cage is both the masonry cylinder and, in joinery, the timber prism formed by the montants.

english: the enclosing cylindrical wall of a vis; also a cul-de-four cap over a round vis
definition: QUOTATION REPAIRED: the full text is 'avec DEUX ET DEMI DE giron pres de la coquille qui l'environnoit' (Sauval on the Louvre); the reader's shorter version was a paraphrase inside quotation marks. Second sense verbatim: 'La ronde est couverte d'une voute en cul-de-four ou coquille.' NOTE: 30 occurrences, mostly in the sense of light or of an openwork screen. Viollet does not use jour for the open well; he says 'un vide'.

[Escalier] The level platform at a floor or between flights. 25 occurrences. 'un palier d'entresol A'; 'le palier de premier etage B'. NOTE: Rule: 'les hauteurs des paliers pussent concorder avec les hauteurs des planchers'. || [Maison] In fig 3 the first landing carries a bench, the second is closed in front of the solid entrance door.

english: landing tread, the step that forms part of the landing
definition: [Escalier] In timber stairs, the last step of a flight doubling as the landing member, halved into the post and part-borne on a poutrelle. 8 occurrences. NOTE: Key joint in fig.27/28; bolted through the gousset.

[Escalier] The raking beam carrying the steps, into which they are tenoned. 25 occurrences. Straight (limon droit) or helical (limon spirale). NOTE: In fig.32 a limon spirale assembled into the step abouts carries the rotating cylindrical partition.

[Escalier] Worked in the solid of a stone or timber newel ('la main-courante prise dans la masse'), or framed into the posts in a timber stair ('leurs mains-courantes dans les poteaux'). NOTE: In the newel-less vis the handrail is the stack of boudins on the step ends instead.

english: roll moulding; here the rolled inner end of a newel-less winder
definition: [Escalier] 'portaient chacune un boudin a leur extremite, pres du centre, pour offrir une main-courante'. NOTE: One occurrence but structurally decisive: the boudins stacked in a helix ARE the handrail.

[Escalier] 5 occurrences; can be pierced/turned (fig.16, 17, 27) or 'pleine' (solid, panelled) as at the Chambre des comptes. NOTE: Posts (poteaux de balustrades / montants) tenon into the limon, rails into the corner posts.

english: perron, external flight/platform giving access to a piano nobile / external stair and platform up to a raised door
definition: [Escalier] Explicitly NOT to be confused with an escalier exterieur: 'les escaliers exterieurs (qu'il ne faut pas confondre avec les perrons)'. NOTE: Great halls were reached 'par de larges perrons' (Paris, Poitiers) — a wide monumental external approach, not a stair serving storeys. || [Maison] 'ces escaliers exterieurs, ou grands perrons, jouent un role important dans les habitations des XIe et XIIe siecles.' NOTE: Cross-referenced to the article Perron.

english: to dress off, to bevel away; a step whose underside is dressed to a smooth rake
definition: [Escalier] 6 occurrences. 'les marches delardees par dessous', 'toutes les marches sont par dessous delardees'. NOTE: Produces the plafond rampant. This is why a medieval vis has a smooth helical soffit rather than a stepped one.

[Escalier] The sloping underside formed by the dressed step undersides: 'Ces marches seront delardees par-dessous et formeront plafond rampant.' NOTE: Generator: the soffit is a helicoid, not a staircase; two occurrences.

The three-state enum {delarde, chanfreine, angles vifs} IS textually grounded; the cost reading is the reader's inference. || SOURCE ENTRIES: [Escalier] The cheaper alternative to delarder: 'les marches sont chanfreinees par-dessous ainsi qu'on le voit en D' — done to improve the echappement. NOTE: Three states available to a generator: delarde (smooth), chanfreine (chamfered), or a angles vifs (left square).

english: to cut a twisted/warped shape out of the solid
definition: [Escalier] The shaping of a solid winder from a log or block: 'Ce debillardement des marches ne perd aucune des parties solides'; 'les marches debillardees, pleines'. NOTE: 3 occurrences. A specific stereotomy/joinery verb worth keeping.

english: the overlap of one step over the next
definition: [Escalier] 'Les recouvrements sont indiques par lignes ponctuees'; 'Les espaces EF donnent le recouvrement des marches l'une sur l'autre'. NOTE: In fig.9 and fig.30 the overlap is drawn dotted — a drawing convention that also encodes the joint.

[Escalier] 'il avait encore l'avantage de relier le noyau avec la cage par toutes ces marches qui formaient autant d'etresillons'. NOTE: One occurrence but a first-class structural claim: the treads brace the newel against the cage wall.

[Escalier] The vault under the earliest medieval vis: 'un berceau en spirale bati en moellon, reposant sur le noyau et sur le parement circulaire interieur'. NOTE: Dropped from the beginning of the XIII c. Viollet notes the sommiers of a raking vault are slow to set out, waste much stone and need special care in setting.

english: lagging, the boarding over the centring on which small rubble is laid / lagging, boarding over centering
definition: [Escalier] 'grossierement faites en petits moellons maconnes sur couchis'. NOTE: Two occurrences; the thing the XIII c. method eliminates, along with the cintres. || [Construction -- Voutes] The boards laid from centering to centering to carry the masonry. NOTE: Its ABSENCE is the point: 'l'on procede de suite a la construction des voutes sans couchis'.

english: centring, formwork arch / centering, formwork arch
definition: [Escalier] 'Ce procede evitait les cintres, les couchis, une main-d'oeuvre assez longue sur le tas.' NOTE: The economic argument for the self-supporting step. || [Construction -- Voutes] Timber arch supporting masonry until it closes. NOTE: 'les causes de depenses les plus importantes... ce sont les cintrages de bois'.

english: springer (the lowest voussoir of an arch or vault)
definition: [Escalier] 'un petit epaulement H pour recevoir les sommiers du berceau'. NOTE: Bears on the newel epaulement one side, notched into the cage wall the other. || [Construction -- Voutes] The lowest stone(s) of an arch, at the springing. NOTE: In Gothic practice one stone contains the interpenetrating starts of several ribs.

[Escalier] The shoulder cut to receive a bearing — on a newel drum for the vault springer, or under a step mortise in a timber newel to relieve the bearing. NOTE: Same word does duty in stone and timber; a generator can treat it as one feature.

english: drum (a course of a cylindrical newel)
definition: [Escalier] 'Les tambours du noyau portent un petit epaulement H'; 'Voici, fig. 8, comme sont tailles les tambours du noyau'. NOTE: The unit of the early newel.
[Escalier] The Chateaudun newel 'est monte en assises hautes'. NOTE: A dating/quality signal for XV c. newels.

english: set on edge, against the natural bed of the stone / set on edge / against the natural bed, cross-bedded
definition: [Escalier] 'on composa les noyaux de grandes pierres en delit comme on le fait pour les poteaux des vis en charpente'; the Reims chandelles are 'des morceaux de pierres en delit'. NOTE: 3 occurrences. Explicit analogy: a stone newel in delit imitates a timber post. || [Construction -- Voutes] A stone laid so its natural bed is vertical. NOTE: Used for monolithic shafts to get rigidity: 'comme des chandelles de charpente' (like timber props). Viollet treats it as a deliberate stiffening device.
[Escalier] 'relies entre eux au moyen de forts goujons de pierre dure' — the Tremoille newel's three superposed stones. NOTE: Hardstone dowels, not iron.

english: band, fillet — here the helical fillet on a newel receiving the step ends
definition: [Escalier] 'Ces noyaux porterent des mains-courantes prises dans la masse et des saillies en forme de bandeau spirale, pour recevoir les petits bouts des marches'; fig.20 label B. NOTE: Two helices at one pitch on the same newel: handrail above, bandeau below.

english: housing, the sinking into which a step end is set
definition: [Escalier] fig.20: 'le bandeau recevant les marches dont l'incrustement est indique dans notre dessin'. NOTE: Also 'encastrements' for the Tremoille newel.

english: squinch, corner arch spanning across an angle
definition: [Escalier] The device that turns a square cage into an octagon or circle: 'Dans les angles du carre des trompes arrivent a une corniche spirale et soutiennent les marches d'angles'. NOTE: 5 occurrences. At Chateaudun they are appareillees as slightly inclined plates-bandes because the stair is large.

english: small squinch cut from a single stone
definition: [Escalier] 'les trois angles droits restant a l'interieur etaient, sous les marches, garnis de trompillons pris dans une seule pierre sculptee'. NOTE: 2 occurrences; fig.19. The small-stair version of a trompe.
[Escalier] At Chateaudun, 'des culs-de-lampe poses aux angles de l'octogone portent la corniche spirale'. Also used for the little corbels carrying torches. NOTE: 3 occurrences.

[Escalier] The ring at the top of the trompes: 'la corniche spirale, dont la projection horizontale etant un cercle parfait soutient les bouts des marches'. NOTE: The load-transfer ring of the square-cage type. Its horizontal projection is a true circle.

[Escalier] 'L'escalier de l'hotel de la Tremoille a Paris donnait en plan un carre avec un grand pan abattu'; also 'un pan abattu de facon a donner en projection horizontale un octogone a quatre grands cotes et a quatre plus petits'. NOTE: 2 occurrences. Gives the irregular octagon: four long sides, four short.

english: outside the main block, projecting clear of the ranges
definition: [Escalier] 'maitre Raimond le jeta entierement hors-d'oeuvre en dedans la cour'; 'en placant ainsi les grands escaliers hors-oeuvre, ils ne derangeaient pas les distributions interieures'. NOTE: The single most important planning term in the article.

english: spine wall, internal dividing wall / internal cross wall / spine wall
definition: [Escalier] The wall separating the two flights of the Roman stair: 'deux rampes separees par un mur de refend'. NOTE: One occurrence, fig.1. || [Maison] Carries the joists and, in 12th-c houses, the corbelled front timber frame. NOTE: Viollet read the surviving refend wall-heads to prove the lost timber upper storeys.

english: upright, stile — the post carrying one step of a joinery vis
definition: [Escalier] 'Chaque marche possedait son montant dans lequel elle venait s'assembler. Ces montants, d'un seul morceau pour chaque etage, etaient assembles au pied dans un plateau en charpente, et au sommet dans un cercle.' NOTE: One per step, so the timber cage is a prism with as many faces as steps.
[Escalier] Tenoned onto the renfort, part-carrying the marche paliere. NOTE: fig.27/28 labels C, C-prime.

english: long bracket, gallows-brace / bracket, raking strut
definition: [Escalier] The long brackets relieving the first steps off the rotating newel: 'elle est puissamment soulagee ainsi que les trois suivantes par des potences I'. NOTE: 2 occurrences; replaced higher up by shorter liens 'afin de faciliter le degagement'. || [Maison] The Reims facade is corbelled 'sur cinq fortes potences'.
[Escalier] 'assemblees dans le limon a tenons et mortaises' — the universal step-to-string joint in medieval timber stairs. NOTE: Steps are never simply housed and nailed.
[Escalier] 'Ces marches etant pleines sont prises, habituellement, dans des billes de bois' — an oak log 0,50 m in diameter. NOTE: The raw stock unit for wooden steps.

english: slab, outer waste board from a log
definition: [Escalier] 'il reste en M de belles dosses que l'on peut utiliser ailleurs'. NOTE: The by-product of the six-triangle conversion.

english: base plate / head ring (of a joinery vis cage)
definition: [Escalier] The montants are framed at the foot into a plateau and at the head into a cercle, both in carpentry. NOTE: The two rings that make the timber cage rigid.

english: secured in the mortise with obliquely driven pegs (provisional)
definition: TRANSLATION UNRESOLVED, and the flag must stay. 'Le boulon d'axe excepte, ces escaliers etaient brandis et maintenus assembles sans le secours de ferrures.' In French carpentry brandir a tenon means to secure it in its mortise with pegs or nails driven OBLIQUELY - a specific operation with a modelling consequence (angled peg holes through the tenon), not a vague 'racked together'. Viollet gives no BRANDIR article and the word does not occur in Charpente, Maison, Serrurerie or Voutes, so it cannot be settled from him. Do NOT let 'without ironwork' harden into 'without pegs': chevilles are not ferrures. || SOURCE ENTRIES: [Escalier] 'le boulon d'axe excepte, ces escaliers etaient brandis et maintenus assembles sans le secours de ferrures'. NOTE: Uncertain-translation flag: brandi here means the frame was drawn up and held by its own joints.

english: the circumvolving stair — the outer of two concentric vis
definition: [Escalier] 'La vis interieure devenait escalier de service, et le degre circonvolutant, escalier d'honneur.' NOTE: One occurrence. Names a status distinction a game can use: inner = service, outer = honour.

english: double helix (two interleaved flights in one cage)
definition: [Escalier] 'ces grandes vis de palais etaient a double revolution, de sorte que l'on pouvait descendre par l'une et remonter par l'autre sans se rencontrer et meme sans se voir'. NOTE: One occurrence in that exact form; the Bernardins and fig.29 are the examples.

[Escalier] Named in Sauval's description of Saint-Mederic (Saint-Merri), Paris: 'Il existait deux vis de Saint-Gille dans les deux tourelles'. NOTE: Viollet does NOT define the term in this article. Do not gloss it further from this source; conventionally it denotes a vis with a helical vault over it, after the example at Saint-Gilles-du-Gard, but that is not stated here.

[Escalier] The slender stones relieving the outer step ends at Reims: 'Des chandelles de pierre B viennent soulager les portees A'; 'les pierres B ne sont qu'une suite d'etancons formant cloture a jour'. NOTE: One occurrence each. Structurally a screen, not a load path. || [Construction -- Voutes] A vertical timber strut, used by Viollet as the analogy for an en-delit shaft.

english: liais — a hard fine Paris limestone
definition: [Escalier] 'les carrieres de liais de Paris n'avaient pu fournir a la fois un nombre de morceaux de la dimension voulue'. NOTE: The stone whose block size limited step length at the Louvre.

english: flat lintel-arch, a straight arch of jointed stones / flat lintel course / raking flat course
definition: [Escalier] The Chateaudun trompes are 'des plates-bandes legerement inclinees vers l'angle'. NOTE: Spelled as plates-bandes in the plural in the text. || [Maison] The Vitteaux turret is carried on a well-coursed plate-bande rampante instead of on the tread ends.

english: the end / butt of a timber or of a course
definition: [Maison] 'la cage est posee sur l'about des marches formant encorbellement' - the stair cage rides on the projecting ends of the treads. NOTE: Key word for the Burgundian corbelled turret.

english: masonry pier at the end of a timber frame

[Maison] Squared trunks piled on one another and notched (embreves) at the returns; still practised in Switzerland and among Slav peoples in Viollet's day.
