[Maison] The great first-floor hall of Jacques Coeur 'possedait une estrade comme les grandes salles des chateaux'. NOTE: The clearest single point of contact with the English hall.
[Maison] Timber lean-tos of one storey ring the small courts at Montreal; open lean-tos shade the Languedoc farmhouse.
[Maison] 'K est une salle ouverte, sorte de preau couvert sous la chapelle' at the hotel de Cluny.
[Maison] Around the bastide square, 'tres-larges, bas'; suppressed in the 15th c because the posts were an encumbrance.
[Maison] At the angles of the bastide square, letting carts enter diagonally; the storeys above are corbelled over them.
[Maison] 'Un ilot des maisons de la ville de Montpazier fait voir avec quelle uniformite cellulaire ces habitations sont construites.'

english: planted new town of the 13th c
definition: [Maison] Built at one go on granted land following the indication of the ingenieurs, with wide franchises; regular plans drawn to the line, with squares, markets, churches, fountains and ramparts, and equal lotting. NOTE: Viollet lists roughly 30 by name, dated 1260-1330.

english: the layout engineer of a bastide
definition: [Maison] 'suivant l'indication des ingenieurs' - the term Viollet uses for the men who set out the plans.
[Maison] 'maisons avec ou sans allees couvertes, mais baties d'apres un lotissement egal.'

english: Norman rural plot, longer than wide
definition: [Maison] 'On assignait donc aux colons des boels, ordinairement plus longs que larges... A l'une des extremites du boel, chacun elevait sa chaumiere.' NOTE: Quoted from L. Delisle via du Cange; the ancestor of the village street.
[Maison]
[Maison] Still mentioned by Gregory of Tours; gone by the 12th c, when 'la famille se reunit autour du meme foyer'. NOTE: A dating rule for interior programme.

[Maison] Usual in Languedoc in the middle ages as still in Viollet's day; replaced in Normandy from the 13th c by the bail a terme (fixed-term lease). NOTE: Given as the economic cause of the differing quality and rate of change of rural houses.

[Maison] Built in cemeteries, free of all secular jurisdiction, refuges for pilgrims and the sick under the supervision of religious; 'Ces maisons se reconnaissaient a des croix de bois fichees sur leur comble.' NOTE: A discrete, instantly recognisable building type: put wooden crosses on the roof.

[Construction -- Voutes] The projecting stone rib on the diagonal of a vault cell. Viollet is emphatic that this, not the pointed arch, is the 'veritable nom' of the member. NOTE: CRITICAL FALSE FRIEND. In Viollet 'ogive' NEVER means 'pointed arch'; a pointed arch is 'tiers-point' or 'arc brise'. Mistranslating this wrecks every passage.

[Construction -- Voutes] A vault whose cells are carried by an independent armature of diagonal and transverse stone arches. NOTE: Viollet's technical term for the Gothic system proper, as opposed to a merely ribbed dome ('coupole nervee').
[Construction -- Voutes] The arch spanning across the bay, from pier to pier, at right angles to the axis.
[Construction -- Voutes] The extra transverse arch that cuts a square (sexpartite) bay into two. NOTE: Its rise must equal the radius of the semicircular diagonal (fig. 55).
[Construction -- Voutes] The arch lying against the wall, bounding the cell on the wall side. NOTE: In the French method this is the member that COMMANDS the web course count.
[Construction -- Voutes] Generic term for any rib standing proud of the vault surface. NOTE: Viollet uses it for Roman brick ribs buried in the mass as well as for Gothic ribs.

[Construction -- Voutes] A rib run along the crown line of the vault, from the crown of one arch to the crown of another. NOTE: Viollet derives it functionally: it exists to receive and mask the overlapping ends of web courses.

[Construction -- Voutes] An intermediate rib springing with the others but landing on a ridge rib rather than at the vault crown. NOTE: Viollet derives it functionally too: to stop near-flat web courses from sagging at mid-length.
[Construction -- Voutes] The masonry filling a cell between the ribs. NOTE: In the Ile-de-France method it is thin rubble (moellon), 0.10-0.12 m thick.

[Construction -- Voutes] One triangular panel of web treated as an independent little vault. NOTE: Key to Viollet's doctrine: 'Chaque triangle de la voute francaise est une cellule independante se maintenant d'elle-meme.'
[Construction -- Voutes] Small hand-laid stone; 'pique' = pick-dressed. NOTE: Web unit width 0.08-0.15 m; thickness 0.10-0.12 m.
[Construction -- Voutes] One of the wedge stones of an arch.

[Construction -- Voutes] The stack of horizontally bedded courses at the springing, out of which the ribs progressively emerge. NOTE: 'c'est-a-dire presentassent de veritables assises a lits horizontaux, afin de resister a la pression'.
[Construction -- Voutes] A single horizontal layer of masonry.

[Construction -- Voutes] The natural bed thickness of the quarry stone, which fixes the course height. NOTE: 'Il s'agit de diviser la hauteur PQ en un certain nombre d'assises, suivant la hauteur des bancs.' - i.e. the material, not the design, sets the number of springer courses.
[Construction -- Voutes] The face on which a stone rests or which it presents. NOTE: 'lits horizontaux' = horizontal beds; 'lit inferieur/superieur' = lower/upper bed.

english: joint normal to the curve, radial joint
definition: [Construction -- Voutes] A joint plane perpendicular to the arch curve, i.e. radial. NOTE: Used only ABOVE the tas-de-charge, once a rib has freed itself.

english: soffit face, intrados face of a voussoir or course
definition: [Construction -- Voutes] The concave visible face. NOTE: Each French web course has a lens-shaped douelle, wider at mid-length than at its ends.
[Construction -- Voutes] Inner (concave) and outer (convex) surface of an arch or vault. NOTE: The web epure is set out on the EXTRADOS of the ribs, not the intrados.

english: keystone; also the crown, the crown level
definition: [Construction -- Voutes] The stone at the crown; by extension the crown point and its level. NOTE: In this article 'clef' is used far more often as a LEVEL DATUM than as a structural member.
[Construction -- Voutes] The line joining the crowns of the arches bounding a cell.
[Construction -- Voutes] A keystone hanging below the ribs. NOTE: 16th-century; Viollet gives their setting-out by equal division of the lierne branches.
[Construction -- Voutes] Height of an arch crown above its springing line; also the rise of a chord over an arc.
[Construction -- Voutes] An arch struck on a full semicircle.
[Construction -- Voutes] An arch of two circular branches meeting in a point at the crown. NOTE: 'formes d'arcs de cercle brises a la clef'.
[Construction -- Voutes] An arch flatter than a semicircle.
[Construction -- Voutes] To raise the springing of an arch on a vertical stretch before the curve begins. NOTE: The standard device for making unequal spans crown level.
[Construction -- Voutes] A vault whose crown line is inclined rather than level. NOTE: Typical of aisle and gallery vaults where the outer arch is wider than the inner.
[Construction -- Voutes] A bay longer in one direction; here the rectangular bay that replaced the square bay around 1230.
[Construction -- Voutes] One structural division of a building.

[Construction -- Voutes] Two grooved curved boards keyed together so they can be lengthened, hooked onto the ribs by iron squares, on which each web course is turned. NOTE: Boards about 0.04 m thick. THE tool that makes centreless web building possible.
[Construction -- Voutes] A small board curve used instead of a proper centre.
[Construction -- Voutes] Removing the falsework.
[Construction -- Voutes] The geometrical drawing from which templates are taken. NOTE: 'Cette epure ne se fait pas sur le chantier' - the web epure is a theoretical demonstration, not shop practice.
[Construction -- Voutes] The man who draws the epures and issues the templates.

english: coursed ashlar / built in dressed courses
definition: [Construction -- Voutes] Cut-stone masonry laid to courses.
[Construction -- Voutes] A voussoir shaped to its bounding envelope but not yet moulded.
[Construction -- Voutes] The template handed to the stonecutter. NOTE: Must allow for the distortion of the mouldings at each successive bed.
[Construction -- Voutes] The slab over a capital. NOTE: In Gothic practice its plan is DERIVED from the springer bed outline, not chosen; may be square-return or star-shaped.
[Construction -- Voutes] The body of the capital under the abacus. NOTE: The springer front is always set plumb with the upper square of the corbeille.
[Construction -- Voutes] The ring moulding at the top of a shaft. NOTE: One astragal can carry three baskets on a bundled springing.
[Construction -- Voutes] A voussoir with a stepped rebate. NOTE: Explicitly rejected: 'ne peuvent jamais etre bien posees et dont les lits ne sauraient etre exactement remplis de mortier'.
[Construction -- Voutes] The embedded rear end of a voussoir. NOTE: 'ecornant, au besoin, les queues de ces arcs' - clipping the tails; 'affamer les queues' = to starve/undercut them.
[Construction -- Voutes] A doubly ruled non-developable surface. NOTE: Something Gothic setters-out worked hard to avoid; wedge-shaped abaci exist for this reason.

[Construction -- Voutes] The arch carrying thrust from the high vault out to an external buttress. NOTE: Viollet: 'il ne soutire pas cette action oblique' - it does not draw the thrust off, it only opposes its effects.
[Construction -- Voutes] The mass receiving the thrust of an arch or flyer.
[Construction -- Voutes] The external pier reinforcing a wall.
[Construction -- Voutes] Free-standing support.
[Construction -- Voutes] A plain round column, as opposed to a bundle of shafts. NOTE: Viollet claims naves on these deformed less than those on compound piers rising from the floor.
[Construction -- Voutes]

[Construction -- Voutes] The locus of the points where the resultant crosses each bed. NOTE: Viollet's stated equilibrium condition: the curve must nowhere leave the intrados/extrados lines of the arch; its first element at the crown is horizontal for a semicircular arch.
[Construction -- Voutes]
[Construction -- Voutes] Thrust bearing where there is no abutment. NOTE: What the Chalons architect 'craignait' on a small-radius circular plan.

[Construction -- Voutes] Viollet's own coinage: destroying thrust at its origin by opposing a weaker counter-thrust plus a vertical load, so the obliques resolve into a vertical. NOTE: Contrasted with the method of merely CONTAINING the effects.
[Construction -- Voutes] Downward movement of masonry as mortar compresses. NOTE: Viollet builds an entire intentional reading of Chalons on anticipated settlement.
[Construction -- Voutes] A stone wedge closing an angle between two members. NOTE: 'une simple cale a en pierre forme coin entre le tailloir et les claveaux'.
[Construction -- Voutes] A ring tying an en-delit shaft back into the wall.
[Construction -- Voutes] Light stone and mortar poured between ribs and cells. NOTE: The Roman method; also the Burgundian expedient.
[Construction -- Voutes] A thin vault of large flat bricks laid on sparse lagging, which becomes the permanent centering for the real vault. NOTE: The Roman economy trick, from the article Voute.
[Construction -- Voutes]
[Construction -- Voutes] NOTE: 'berceau annulaire' = annular barrel over a curved ambulatory.
[Construction -- Voutes] A vault of two intersecting barrels. NOTE: 'voute d'arete romaine' = the groin vault WITHOUT ribs, curved in all directions.
[Construction -- Voutes] The line where two vault surfaces meet. NOTE: 'arete creuse' / 'angle rentrant' = a hollow, re-entrant arris - the defect the ridge rib hides.
[Construction -- Voutes] The angle member of a polygonal chapel.
[Construction -- Voutes]
[Construction -- Voutes] NOTE: Coursed in concentric rings; the ancestor of both the Aquitaine and the English web.
[Construction -- Voutes] One ring of the ambulatory. NOTE: 'les deux precinctions exterieures devaient alors comprendre un plus grand nombre de piles'.
[Construction -- Voutes]
[Construction -- Voutes] The semicircular or polygonal end of an apse.
[Construction -- Voutes]
[Construction -- Voutes]
[Construction -- Voutes] NOTE: 16th-century vaults are slabs rebated onto rib voussoirs.
[Construction -- Voutes]
[Construction -- Voutes] The groove in which a slab is seated.
[Construction -- Voutes] The only cutting tool the web mason needs, besides his cerce.
[Construction -- Voutes] The moulded arch of an arcade.
[Construction -- Voutes] NOTE: At Mouliherne the ogives are 'que des tores a section demi-circulaire'.
[Construction -- Voutes] Out of plumb by design or by settlement.

[Serrurerie] The beaten-iron or sheet backplate on which the lock mechanism is 'piquees, c'est-a-dire montees et rivees' (pricked, i.e. mounted and riveted). Viollet keeps the word MASCULINE against modern usage: 'Pallatre est aujourd'hui feminin, mais Jousse le fait masculin.' It is also the layer the red cloth sits on: 'Entre ces ornements de fer battu et le pallatre, est appose un morceau de drap rouge.'

[Serrurerie] FALSE FRIEND: Viollet's spelling of pene = the sliding BOLT of a lock. Not 'peel' and not a plate. 'en d , le pele avec ses cramponnets et ses ressorts' (fig. 26). 'pele dormant' = dead bolt (fig. 30).

english: the outside sliding bolt-slide worked by a knob
definition: [Serrurerie] FALSE FRIEND: NOT a modern trigger and NOT a tumbler. It is the slide visible on the outside of the lock, moved by the bouton. Housed under a gaine or coque (fig. 25 section ab).
[Serrurerie] The socket in the door frame that the bolt shoots into. Lettered G on fig. 23 and g on fig. 34.
[Serrurerie] The domed/raised case over the mechanism, held to the pallatre by the estoquiaux. 'serrure a bosse et a pele dormant' (fig. 30).

english: small hook that the key lowers to BLOCK the bolt
definition: [Serrurerie] A stop, not a spring - distinguish it from the ressorts it works against. 'en d , le pele avec ses cramponnets et ses ressorts.'

english: rivets / stays fixing the bosse to the pallatre
definition: [Serrurerie] 'en c , les estoquiaux qui servent a maintenir la bosse de la serrure sur le pallatre.'

english: key-guide wards riveted to the plate
definition: [Serrurerie] 'en b , l'entree du panneton avec ses fouets piques sur le pallatre.'
[Serrurerie] The projecting web of the key that turns in the lock.

[Serrurerie] The latch of a serrure a clenche, pivoting on a tourillon: 'Le mecanisme que donne notre figure se compose d'un loquet a fleau A monte sur un tourillon a.' (fig. 27, Lalinde, late 14th c.)
[Serrurerie] The pin the fleau of a latch swings on.

english: rake (the toothed bar the key drives)
definition: [Serrurerie] Lettered h on fig. 27, pivoting on axis s; its tail bears on the latch at i.
[Serrurerie] The external lever pressed with the thumb to lift a latch.
[Serrurerie] The hooked catch the latch drops into.
[Serrurerie] 'serrure a clenche ou loquet' - a latch-lock. Viollet: 'Des le XVe siecle, on trouve deja des serrures dites a clenche ou loquet', yet he dates fig. 27 to the end of the 14th c.
[Serrurerie] A lock that can be worked from a single face of the door.

english: having TWO keyholes (workable from both sides)
definition: [Serrurerie] The Angers lock of fig. 26 is benarde: 'est a deux entrees'.

english: reinforced base / collar of a lock
definition: [Serrurerie] 'Un morceau de drap rouge garnit egalement le fond sous le feuillage de l'embase de la serrure precedente (fig. 30).'

[Serrurerie] The cut sheet ornament. Load-bearing detail for a generator: the SAME rivets that fix the cut-outs also retain the cloth ground - 'un morceau de drap rouge maintenu par les rivets qui retiennent les decoupures.'

[Serrurerie] A separate LAYER sandwiched between the openwork sheet and the backplate on French lockwork and pull-rings, attested three times (figs 25, 30, 31). Assembly order: pallatre -> cloth -> pierced fer battu -> rivets through all three. NOTE: Viollet is SILENT on tinning - zero occurrences of etame/etamer/etamage/etain/fer-blanc/blanchi/argent in 135,681 characters - so he neither confirms nor contradicts Gardner's 'brightly tinned' finish.

english: gluing of skin, cloth or felt onto a door leaf
definition: [Serrurerie] 'Ces ferrures sont posees sur des peaux marouflees sur le bois et peintes en rouge vif' (Ebreuil, early 12th c) and '...ou une peau, ou un feutre maroufle sur le vantail. D'ailleurs il en etait de meme pour la plupart des pentures, et l'on trouve encore les traces de ces marouflages.' Viollet asserts SURVIVING PHYSICAL TRACES, so this is evidence, and he generalises it to MOST hinge straps - a stronger claim than Gardner's.

[Serrurerie] The medieval term, as against tole (modern rolled sheet), and Viollet flags tole as OUR anachronism: 'des fers battus employes comme ornements, et que nous appellerions aujourd'hui de la tole repoussee'.

english: faggoting / piling of the bloom by repeated welding
definition: [Serrurerie] How medieval bar and plate were actually made, in the absence of rolls: 'autrefois le fer n'arrivait que peu a peu, et par un corroyage repete, de l'etat de lopin a celui de barreau ou de plaque.'

english: hardened-iron swage or sinking die / to swage
definition: [Serrurerie] CRITICAL FALSE FRIEND - etampe is NOT etamer (to tin). Viollet defines it himself: 'C'est une matrice de fer trempe, un coin auquel on a donne en creux la forme de l'objet a etamper.' Reading an etampe passage as a tinned finish converts a hot-forging operation into a surface coating.
[Serrurerie] The hammer under which the bloom was worked: 'lopins de fonte a peine corroyee au martinet'.
[Serrurerie] The starting stock, worked up by corroyage.

[Serrurerie] FALSE FRIEND: this is ROLLING, not English 'laminated' (plied/layered). Viollet uses these words ONLY of modern industry and only to DENY them to the Middle Ages, three separate times. Gardner agrees. Any rendering of medieval French ironwork as 'laminated sheet' inverts the technical sense - what is attested is corroyage plus bands built up from parallel bars soldered only at their ends.

english: strap staple (for a bolt or bar)
definition: [Serrurerie] Lettered B B on fig. 23 and a on fig. 34.
[Serrurerie] The staple a hasp drops over, and the slot in it.
[Serrurerie] The hinged plate that drops over the auberon. Lettered e on fig. 34.
[Serrurerie] Fig. 32.
[Serrurerie] Geared bolt for great gate leaves 'd'une hauteur de 4 a 5 metres', worked by a levier a engrenage c on axe d (fig. 34).

[Serrurerie] The long decorated strap across a door leaf. Built up from parallel bars: 'la bande ou le corps de la penture se compose, pour le collet, de quatre barres ; pour le premier membre, de trois barres... Ces barres, paralleles et jointives, ne sont soudees entre elles qu'a leurs extremites' (figs 12-13).
[Serrurerie] A slender applied rod imitating a twig in beaten-iron foliage.

french: rouge sombre / rouge cerise / rouge blanc
english: dull red / cherry red / white heat
definition: [Serrurerie] Viollet's forging-temperature scale. 'chauffer au rouge blanc' = heat to WHITE HEAT for fire-welding - it does NOT describe a white or tinned surface.

Viollet's own definition: "des bandes de fer clouees et boulonnees aux vantaux des portes, munies d'un oeil entrant dans un gond, destinees a suspendre ces vantaux et a permettre de les faire pivoter facilement sur ces gonds" - iron bands nailed and bolted to the door leaves, fitted with an EYE that goes over a PINTLE, to hang the leaf and let it pivot. NOTE: the penture is the whole strap including its eye; it is NOT the pintle.

english: pintle / hook-pin fixed in the jamb
definition: The male pivot sealed into stone or wood of the jamb. Its projecting nose is the mamelon; behind that a square renfort (shoulder) carries the load; f in fig. 1 is the scellement (the bedding/leading-in of the gond into the masonry).
Jousse: "le bout qui sort dehors la pierre ou bois" - the end that projects out of the stone or wood; the penture's eye is rolled to this diameter.

english: eye (rolled knuckle at the strap's inner end)
definition: b in fig. 1. Made by rolling the end of the flat bar round, to the diameter of the gond's mamelon, then welding the roll shut: "se replie en rond, de la grosseur du mamelon du gond ... qui sera soude si on veut, et arrondi en facon que le gond tourne aisement dedans".

english: collar / neck - the thickened root of the strap next to the eye
definition: c in fig. 1. The heaviest, most difficult part to forge; at Notre-Dame it is built up of FOUR parallel bars. Branches and the securing crampon attach at or behind its renflement (swelling).

d in fig. 1; d' in section B. A staple passing OVER the collet behind its swelling, through the whole thickness of the door, riveted on the far side (double rivure at e). This is the primary structural fixing, not the nails.

english: false penture / dummy strap (a decorative-structural band that carries no pivot)
definition: A band independent of the hinge proper, without eye or gond, whose job is to tie all the door's boards together: "une bande independante de la penture, et appelee fausse penture, rend toutes les frises du vantail solidaires".

english: the vertical boards/planks of the door leaf
definition: The planks the ironwork clamps together. Straps 'give the nose' (donner du nez) i.e. sag, under the weight of the frises if unbraced.

english: to 'give the nose' - to droop/sag at the free end
definition: Viollet's own gloss: "c'est-a-dire de flechir sous le poids des frises" - to bend under the weight of the boards. The multiplied branches exist to prevent this.

english: Flemish band - a strap that wraps BOTH faces of the door
definition: Jousse: two bars welded together, rolled as one to form the eye, then opened apart by the door's thickness and bent square so they grip both faces, "principallement du coste de dehors". Jousse rates them better than plain straps because they take both sides of the door.
The swinging panel.
Line ops in fig. 1. The leaf's edge is often notched (entaille) to reach the back of the rebate, which forces the eye of the penture to be offset (detourne, m in detail C).

french: affamer le bois / affame le fer
english: to starve the wood / to starve the iron
definition: To weaken by removing too much material. The offset eye is made narrower than the strap "pour ne pas trop affamer le bois"; and holes in bands "affame le fer et provoque souvent des brisures" - starve the iron and often cause fractures. This is why nail-eyes are made as scrolled volutes rather than drilled holes.
g in fig. 1: a washer interposed between the gond's square shoulder (renfort carre h) and the eye - i.e. the bearing/wear surface.

english: lining plate / rib (stiffener welded to the main band)
definition: A second bar laid on the band and welded only AT INTERVALS via embrasses, leaving the two irons free between - deliberately, to keep elasticity and gain stiffness without weight.

english: clasp band, collar-strap (welded-on ring or wrap over a joint)
definition: The strap-clasp that both joins bundled bars and hides the weld beneath. Structural AND ornamental.

Viollet defines it: "une matrice de fer trempe, un coin auquel on a donne en creux la forme de l'objet a estamper" - a hardened iron matrix, a wedge sunk with the intaglio form of the object. All the folioles and buttons of a bouquet were struck in etampes. NOTE false friend: etamper = to swage/stamp; etamer = to tin.
Unit of the vegetal hierarchy: brindille -> bouquet -> branche secondaire -> branche principale -> bande.
Assembled off the work, then welded to a branch.
Struck in an etampe; welded over a joint; its weld boss is then swaged into a rosette (O) or an embase (P).
A collar at the springing of a branch, widened to make the weld easier.
Obtained by refouler (upsetting) the iron - driving it back on itself to gather mass - then splitting and shaping it.

english: to upset the iron (drive it back on itself to gather metal)
definition: The manoeuvre that creates a renfort or the two souches of branches out of the parent bar: "il faut refouler le fer de maniere a en faire sortir les deux souches des branches".

english: stump/stub (the root a branch springs from)
definition: Raised out of the parent bar by upsetting, so the branch is welded stub-to-stub rather than onto a flat.

english: to slit/split hot along the edge
definition: Slitting languettes (tongues) along the edges of a flat bar hot, then curling each into a volute - an ornament made WITHOUT any weld.
a in fig. 5, slit along the bar's edges then galbe'd into volutes a'.

english: to give a swelling profile / to curve to a contour
definition: Shaping the slit tongues into volutes.

Used INSTEAD of the file, which Viollet says did not exist for this work: angles were "eleges au burin, sans le secours de la lime, qui n'etait pas employee a cette epoque". Chisel cuts struck as the iron cooled to dark red both consolidate the weld and disguise hammer irregularities - they read as engraving.
Chisel-cutting away the metal that spread sideways under the hammer.

english: greifier - the guild trade that made door furniture (pentures)
definition: Per Etienne Boileau's regulations: greifiers = "faiseurs de fermetures de portes (pentures)", distinct from grossiers (taillandiers, edge-tool makers) and serruriers (lock makers). No trade body existed for grosse serrurerie of building.

french: rouge cerise / rouge blanc / rouge sombre
english: cherry red / white heat / dark red
definition: The differential-heat rule for welding one piece onto another: lower piece at cherry red, upper piece at white heat; hammer light blows first, harder as it cools. If both are at white heat "on risquerait, au premier coup de marteau, de ne plus rien trouver sur l'enclume" - one risks finding nothing left on the anvil.

First operation: draw the penture full size, "grandeur d'execution", as pattern for forging and swaging. Traced on a stone or a plaster slab; the work is laid back onto the pattern after every weld to check curves and lengths.

english: to break the line of a curve (a curve that 'kinks')
definition: The defect to avoid when joining branches: obtaining "des courbes qui se suivent regulierement sans jarreter".
Un martinet mu par un cours d'eau composait tout le materiel d'une usine - a water-driven tilt hammer was the whole plant of a works.
Iron came as forged lopins of middling weight; smiths converted them by arm-power into bars, sheet, and small stock.
Viollet's claim for medieval iron quality: it reached bar only by repeated corroyage, not by one pass through rolls.
The plate carrying the lock; the keyhole (entrée) is pierced in it above the bolt. Filets riveted on it both reinforce it and guide the key in the dark.
The sliding bolt. Fig 24 distinguishes the pêle intérieur p from the pêle extérieur P′, joined by two strong rivets running in a coulisse through the pallâtre.
The externally visible sliding member; can be left free to work like a verrou when the cramponnet is raised.
The catch that a turn of the key lowers to block the bolt, or raises to free it. The actual locking element in a serrure à bosse.
Receives the end of the bolt when the door shuts.
Pierced in the pallâtre above the bolt; these locks generally have only one.
The earliest known type, not before the 12th c: box raised with the hammer, bevelled edges, set on a pallâtre, boss outside the leaf and bolt inside.
Riveted retainer holding the bolt to the plate; fig 23 has two.
Baguette used to reinforce the edges of a pallâtre.
Lateral tongue used to hold small beaten leaves to a loop.
The seating in which a langue-de-carpe is taken.
The dominant joint in pentures, with scarfed ends; Viollet's astonishment is that iron behaved 'like wax or lead' under the heat.
A second bar laid on the hinge band; Viollet's lamination is STRUCTURAL, in the band, welded only at intervals and left free between for stiffness plus elasticity plus lightness.

english: going / tread width of a step
definition: CORRECTED. Viollet's own article Giron: «Est la largeur d'une marche d'escalier. Le giron est dit DROIT lorsque la marche est d'une égale largeur dans toute sa longueur; TRIANGULAIRE lorsque la marche est renfermée dans une cage circulaire. Alors ON MESURE LE GIRON DE LA MARCHE AU MILIEU DE SA LONGUEUR.» So a winder's giron is measured at the MIDDLE of the step's length, i.e. essentially the modern walking line - NOT at the wide/outer end. Supersedes the cycle-17 gloss.
A step of equal width along its whole length (straight flight).
A step enclosed in a circular cage; its giron is measured at mid-length.

Viollet's own article: «Cylindre de pierre ou de bois montant de fond, formant l'axe d'un escalier à vis. Les noyaux sont PLEINS OU ÉVIDÉS, TENANT AUX MARCHES OU INDÉPENDANTS, et dans ce dernier cas portant celles-ci au moyen d'un EMBRÈVEMENT ou d'un REPOS.» A 2x2 parameter matrix plus two named bearing methods.
One of the two ways an independent newel carries its steps.
The other way an independent newel carries its steps.

Viollet's own article: a raking TIMBER piece carrying the steps at the end opposite the wall. HARD NEGATIVE RULE: «Les limons de pierre n'étaient PAS employés dans l'architecture du moyen âge» - stone strings were not used; instead the step revolutions in square or oblong-plan stairs were carried ON ARCHES, «beaucoup plus solide que le système de limons appareillés».
Viollet's own article: the wall on which the steps bear, when that wall does not rise above the stepped levels of the flight.
In the newel-less vis the steps each carry a boudin at their INNER end to serve as a main-courante - the handrail is the step's own moulded end.

english: backed off / dressed to a helical soffit
definition: One of three soffit treatments for vis steps.
At Reims the B stones relieving the step bearings; Viollet states they are only «une suite d'étançons formant clôture à jour» - props forming an open screen, not structure.

english: set on edge / against the bed
definition: Stones bedded against their natural bed, used at Reims to relieve the outer step ends.
The continuous ring of wall and towers round a town or castle. Carcassonne has two concentric ones, with the lices between.
The stretch of wall between two towers. Averages 2-3 m thick before gunpowder; its walk is at most 2 m wide.
The walk along the head of a curtain or round a tower, behind the parapet. Deliberately interrupted at towers so a captured stretch does not give the rest.

english: timber back-walk behind a stone machicolation parapet
definition: Boarded gangway built behind the machicolation wall so men can move and be resupplied without crowding the shooters.
Wall on the outer edge of the walk; 0.50-0.70 m thick, pierced with closely set archeres.
The gap in a crenellated parapet. Fitted with hinged timber shutters (portieres) raised on a ratchet.
The solid block between crenels. Shattered dangerously by iron round shot, which is one reason the crenellated stone crown was abandoned.

english: crenellation, the crenellated crown as a whole
definition: Collective term for the crenel-and-merlon system of a tower or curtain.
Timber shutter on a horizontal axle closing a crenel, raised by a cremaillere (ratchet) to whatever angle the shooter wants.
Shutter or portable shield; at Carcassonne the Visigothic crenels have corbels cut to take mantlet pivots.
Shooting slit. External slit about 0.10 m, internal embrasure 1-1.50 m.
Loop shaped for a crossbow; used interchangeably with archere in this work.
General term for a defensive slit. Viollet judges them better for observation, light and air than for real defence, because the angle out is too acute.
Timber gallery corbelled out from the wall head in wartime only, with a floor slotted for vertical dropping. Left the stone parapet standing behind it.

english: hoarding work, the timber system as built
definition: The assembled hoarding, posts, floor and roof; at the Narbonnaise a double hourdage was set in front of the main machicolation.
Small timber machicolated box thrown out over a threatened point. Glossed by Du Cange as castella lignea.
Stone gallery on corbels with vertical drop-slots. Replaced hourds once incendiary attack made timber untenable.
Stone bracket; stacked in courses to carry a machicolation, spaced 0.70-1.20 m axis to axis.
Opening in the vault of a gate passage for dropping stones and fire on anyone trapped below.
Small corbelled angle turret; at Saint-Nazaire the echauguettes flank the hourds and are themselves flanked by the hourds' side loops.
Look-out turret rising above the roof; at Pierrefonds its open-newel stair doubles as a speaking tube down to the wall walk.
Work projecting from the curtain, square or round, giving flanking fire. Round after the 12th century because rams break the angles of square ones.
Angle tower; built on a larger circle than the others because a salient is the easiest point to attack.

english: spur, beak on a round tower
definition: Pointed spur added to a round tower at the tangent point, forcing the attacker off the dead line and killing the ram's purchase.

english: gorge, rear opening of a work
definition: The rear of a tower or outwork. 'Ouvert a la gorge' means open behind, so it cannot be held against the place if captured.
The splayed base of a wall or tower. Towers solid through the height of the talus cannot be mined, and dropped stones ricochet off it into the attackers.

english: batter, inward inclination of a face
definition: Built with an inward lean; the Vincennes towers are 'baties en fruit par assises de gres dur'.
Rough-left projecting face on ashlar; used at Vincennes low down and near the top.
The dressed stonework. Pierrefonds keeps a uniform 0.33 m (one pied) course throughout.
Horizontal layer of masonry; a strong dating and quality signal in this work.
Flint or rubble set in mortar between two dressed facings; the Roman method, kept at Arques.
Dry or wet ditch; 15 m by 7 m at Salses, about 20 m wide at Cadillac, 12 m at Villeneuve-sur-Yonne.

english: scarp, inner face of the ditch
definition: The defender's side of the ditch.

english: counterscarp, outer face of the ditch
definition: The attacker's side of the ditch; the breaching batteries are pushed as close to it as possible.
The open swept slope beyond the counterscarp; the outer tower loops are set to graze it.

english: lists, the ward between two enceintes
definition: The road between outer and inner enceinte. Palisaded off in sections so it cannot be run along; only the night patrols pass the barriers.
Advanced work covering a gate, allowing sorties and covered retreats. Timber and earth until the 13th century, then masonry, always open at the gorge.
Late-medieval broad low work, usually before a gate, built to carry and to resist guns.
Detached fortified block covering a gate, as at the porte Saint-Lazare of Avignon.

english: bastille, detached fort astride a road
definition: A gate or bridge work turned into an independent fort; also the besieger's field fort.
Low outer wall in front of the main rampart, later flanked and used for grazing fire; the artillery-age replacement of the lices.
Covered passage across or along a ditch, loopholed for musketry; used at Salses to link the detached flanking towers to the curtain casemates.
Small low salient work in the ditch bottom for arquebusiers or crossbowmen.
Raised gun platform behind a curtain or on a bastion, giving a second tier of fire.
Rounded shoulder masking a bastion flank.
Detached triangular work before a curtain.
Low work in the ditch before a curtain.
Earth-filled wicker cylinder used to raise emergency parapets.
Woven brushwood layered with earth to build a field rampart.
Stake fence; doubled rows a pike-length apart with the ditch spoil packed between.
Natural or made mound carrying an isolated tower; Viollet traces the type back to late Roman frontier posts.

english: chemise, mantle wall round a donjon
definition: Low wall enclosing the base of a donjon, with its own ditch; at Coucy the gap is 8 m wide and paved.
Internal dividing wall in a rectangular donjon, common in the Norman type.
Any opening at ground level. The article splits fortified gates, donjon and postern doors, abbey, church and house doors.
Small secondary door, usually raised above outside ground and reached by ladder or a single-arm drawbridge.
Raised postern served by an inclined plane and cable winch so the place can be provisioned without opening the main gate.
Grille dropping in a slot; usually doubled, with the two winches deliberately separated to make treachery harder.
The vertical channel a portcullis runs in.
Drum with cranks working the portcullis or drawbridge chains against counterweights.
Weight balancing a portcullis or bridge so two men can work it.
Timber door leaf; usually ironbound and barred, and usually doubled behind the portcullis.
The rebate in the jamb that a leaf or a raised bridge deck closes into.
Deck pivoting on trunnions, raised by chains from two counterweighted arms that swing back into grooves in the face.
Bridge pivoting about a mid axle, the tail dropping into a pit; used at the Coucy donjon door with a hinged ladder flap in the deck.
Light bridge that can be lifted away entirely.
The planked deck of a bridge.
Timber carrying the fixed deck, seated on stone corbels so it can be struck away.
Raking timber trestle carrying a fixed bridge span; dropped by knocking out its keys.
The recess in the wall face that a drawbridge arm swings into.
Timber barrier across an approach or across the lices.
Pivoting counterweighted pole barrier.
Working away the wall foot under cover; the main pre-gunpowder breaching method, answered by the talus and by solid tower bases.
Tunnel driven under a tower, the roof shored with timber and then fired to collapse it.
Rolling timber tower built taller than the wall; useless until the defenders' hourds are burnt or broken.
Timber gallery hide-covered, pushed to the wall foot to protect the ram and the sappers.
The battering ram; still in evidence in French manuscripts through the 15th century.
Trebuchet-class machine; accurate and terrible to 150-200 m by his account.
Stone-throwing engines mounted on the tower platforms.
Gunpowder artillery; from the mid 14th century it slowly overturns the whole system.
Large gun throwing a stone ball on a high trajectory; poor at breaching thick, well-built masonry.
Late 14th and 15th century pieces, mounted on outworks rather than on the old towers.
Missiles shot through the archeres and from the hoardings.
Besieger's line facing the place; also used by the defenders as an outer stockaded line.
Zig-zag trench pushing the batteries towards the counterscarp; Viollet credits the Bureau brothers with the first judicious use.
